Wind Energy Potential 
*304. SHRIPARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the Minister 
of NON-CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India is the fifth largest producer of wind 
energy in the world; 
(b) if so, the percentage of wind energy potential being tapped in the 
country; and 
(c) the proposals to enhance the wind energy in the current Five Year 
Plan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI M. KANNAPPAN): (a) to 
(c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The total wind power installed capacity of 1702 MW is about 13% of 
the present exploitable technical potential of about 13,000 MW. 
(c) The strategy to achieve the goal of 1500 MW of wind power capacity 
addition during the current Five Year Plan will focus on accelerated commercial 
development through industry participation and private investments, supported 
by a conducive policy and regulatory framework. The proposals include fiscal 
and promotional incentives from Government and soft loans from Indian 
Renewable Energy Development Agency (IREDA); attractive policies in 
States for grid connection and sale of electricity generated from wind power 
projects; establishment of a strong local manufacturing base; technical support by 
the Centre for Wind Energy Technology (C-WET); and detailed wind resource 
assessment to identify further potential sites in various States.

*305. SHRI MUNAVVAR HASAN: Will the Minister of COAL AND 
MINES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that many of the officers of Jayant and Khariya 
Projects of Northern Coalfields Limited, Singrauli have not vacated their 
Government quarters despite being transferred to other places many years ago; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that most of the officers and employees 
working under Jayant and Khariya Project have not been provided 
Government quarters so far; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) by when Government quarters are likely to be got vacated from 
officers transferred elsewhere? 
THE MINISTER OF COAL AND MINES (SUSHREE UMA BHARTI): 
(a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) During the period from April, 1996 to 30.11.2002, out of 173 
officers transferred from Jayant Project, only 55 officers are still retaining 
their accommodation at Jayant. Similarly out of 87 officers transferred from

†*307. SHRIMOTILAL VORA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the quantum of fly ash emitted per day accumulated so far from 
Suratgarh SuperThermal Power Station; 
(b) the names of the other Thermal Power Stations which are emitting huge 
quantity of fly ash; 
(c) whether Government have formulated any scheme to make use of such 
fly ash; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) 
to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) According to Rajasthan Rajya Vidyut Utpadan Nigam, the quantum of fly 
ash emitted per day from Suratgarh SuperThermal Power Station in Rajasthan is 
4100 Metric Tonne. The quantum of fly ash accumulated at this Power Station 
upto October, 2002 was 28.366 lakh Metric Tonne. 
(b) The names of the other Thermal Power Stations which are emitting huge 
quantity of fly ash are given in the Statement-I (See below). 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) to (e) A Fly Ash Mission was set up in 1994 promote the utilization of fly 
ash in the country by generating confidence in user agencies regarding feasible 
modes of utilization of fly ash in the country. The Mission has been playing a 
useful catalytic role in increasing the utilization of fly ash in the country. 
Ministry of Environment & Forests (MOEF) have issued a Gazette 
Notification dated 14.09.1999 regarding utilization of fly ash. The 
Notification, inter-alia, requires 100% utilization of fly ash for all new power 
plants within 9 years as well as 100% use of fly ash for all existing power plants 
within 15 years. The Notification enjoins upon the thermal power plants to 
draw up the action plan for utilization/disposal of the fly ash. 
At present, about 19 Million Tonne of fly ash constituting 22% of the 
fly ash produced in the country is being utilized. This has increased from 2.739 
Million Tonne of fly ash constituting about 6.61 % in 1995-96.

*310. SHRIK. RAHMAN KHAN: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the sanctioned strength of National Security Guards (NSG) and the 
number of vacant posts as on 1 st July, 2002; and 
(b) what steps have been taken to modernise the force, increase its 
sanctioned strength and fill up the vacant posts, in view of the increased role of 
the NSG in the present context? 
THE DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER, INCHARGE OFTHE MINISTRY 
OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L.K. ADVANI): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
NSG was raised as a contingency deployment force to deal with terrorist 
activities in various states and anti-hijacking operations. The force is trained and 
equipped to meet these challenges. 
NSG is a 100% deputationist force drawing personnel from the Army, 
Central Para Military Forces (CPMFs) and other Police Organisations. The 
sanctioned strength of NSG is 7330 personnel. There were 1202 vacant posts 
as on 1st July, 2002. The Army, CPMFs and other Police Organisations have 
been advised to sponsor adequate number of personnel to fill up the vacant posts. 
The recent enhancement of NSG allowance is expected to reduce the level of 
vacancies. 
A modernisation plan entailing total expenditure of Rs. 82.49 crores over a 
period of 5 years commencing from the year 2002-03 has been approved for 
NSG. Out of this, Rs. 14.83 crores have been sanctioned during the current 
financial year. 
No change in the role of NSG or increase in its sanctioned strength is 
contemplated at present.

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) 
Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The transmission and distribution (T&D) losses in the 
developed countries of the world are in the range of 6-11%. The level of T&D 
losses in the country is around 31% and is higher than that of the developed 
countries of the world. While the losses in Extra High Voltage network (EHV)

†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
37 

RAJYA SABHA [11 December, 2002] 
The reasons for high T&D losses in the country are on account of: 
i. weak and inadequate sub-transmission and distribution system due to 
low priority being given to these works 
ii. large scale rural electrification programme undertaken in the 
country resulting in long lines and extension of distribution 
network without strengthening the back-up transmission and sub-
transmission system 
iii. too many transformation stages resulting in higher component of 
transformation losses 
iv. improper load management resulting in over loading of system 
v. lower power factor due to pumping load in rural areas, and air 
conditioners, coolers and industrial loads in urban areas and 
inadequate reactive compensation at the load points 
vi. low quality of construction and inadequate maintenance of 
equipment 
vii. unmetered supply to agricultural pumps and small domestic 
connections to weaker sections of the society in some states 
viii. pilferage and theft of energy. 
In order to achieve commercial viability, Ministry of Power has 
formulated a six level intervention strategy that encompasses initiatives at 
national level, state level, SEB/Utility level, distribution circle level, feeder 
level and the consumer level. This six level intervention strategy will focus on 
accountability, deliverability and performance at all levels to rejuvenate the 
distribution sector, where the maximum interface with the ultimate customers 
exists, the highest value addition occurs, and eighty percent of total T&D 
losses including nearly all the commercial losses take place. 
To give a strong impetus to the process of reforms, the Ministry of Power 
organized a Conference of Chief Ministers/Power Ministers on Power Sector 
Reforms on 3rd March 2001. It was emphasised inter alia that commercial 
viability has to be achieved in distribution in 2-3 years through any or all of the 
following 
— Creating profit centres with full accountability 
— Handing over local distribution to Panchayats/Local Bodies/ 
Franchisees/Users Association, wherever necessary 
38 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
— Privatisation of distribution 
25 States have signed Memorandum of Understanding for undertaking 
reforms and restructuring in a time bound manner and linking the support of 
Government of India to achievement of predetermined milestones.To bring 
about commitment towards distribution reforms, State Electricity Boards/Utilities 
have been asked to sign a Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) with Ministry of 
Power as a pre-requisite for release of Accelerated Power Development and 
Reforms Programme (APDRP) funds. Till now 18 States have signed the MoA. A

Studies carried out to find diamond mines 
2107. DR.T.SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
           SHRI NANDIYELLAIAH: 
Will the Minister of COAL AND MINES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether seven international companies which have carried out field 
studies scanning for diamond mines in Madhya Pradesh, Kamataka and 
Chhattisgarh including Andhra Pradesh have found that Andhra Pradesh will 
be the place where researchers could stumble upon diamond mines; 
(b) if so, whether any full report have been received from these 
companies; and 
(c) if so, to what extent diamond mines have been found in these States? 
58 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL AND 
MINES (SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): (a) to (c) Under Section 5(1) of 
the Mines and Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act), 
only an Indian national or a company registered in India can be granted a 
reconnaissance permit for exploration of minerals. On the recommendations of 
the State Governments approvals have been given by the Central Government 
under Section 5(1) of the MM (D&R) Act, 1957 for grant of reconnaissance 
permits in favour of private Indian companies many of which are subsidiaries 
formed by multinational companies. 58 Reconnaissance Permits have been 
approved for diamond and associated minerals in Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, 
Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Orissa States. 
The concept of reconnaissance permit has been introduced in the Act with 
effect from 20.12.1999. Reconnaissance Permits are granted for a period of 
three years. The full report of the work undertaken by the reconnaissance 
permit holder is required to be submitted by him within three months of the 
expiry of the permit or abandonment of operations or termination of the permit 
whichever is earlier. The first approval for grant of reconnaissance permit has 
been conveyed by the Central Government on 25.7.2000 and hence final reports 
are yet to be received by Indian Bureau of Mines, from reconnaissance permit 
holders.

Safety at Defence Depots 
2110. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Will the Minister of DEFENCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the spate of blasts and fire at various defence 
depots and research centres have been due to human errors;

checks the safety measures in such centres and depots;

number of such inspections conducted by (a) Government Officials, (b) Army 
Officials in a year; and

60 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) 
The fire incidents, which have occurred at Ordnance Depots, have been 
investigated. Probable causes of fire in the Ordnance Depots, on analysis of 
past cases, are as under: - 
(i) Fires due to spontaneous combustion. 
(ii) Electrical Short-circuit. 
(Hi) Accidental explosions during testing/repair/breakdown of 
ammunition. However, human element had not been ruled out.

basis. Last inspections were conducted during 2001. In addition, local 
inspections under the aegis of Formation Commander/Depot Commandants 
are conducted as per schedule. Regarding research centres, Centre for 
Environment & Explosive Safety (CEE S) undertakes annual visit to the 
research centres maintained by Defence Researach Development Organisation 
(DRDO), Directorate General of Ordnance Factory (DGOF), Directorate 
General of Quality Assurance (DGQA) and Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL) 
and points out the measures to improve safety. 
(d) During inspection it is ensured that prescribed safety norms are being 
followed and implemented by the laboratories/establishments. The inspecting 
officers have reported about deficiency of equipment and manpower in 
depots on which necessary action has been taken. The implementation of the 
report in respect of the research centres is ensured through periodical reports.

Action regarding streamlining madarsas functioning in India 
2140. SHRINANDIYELLAIAH: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in the light of Pakistan clamping down on all the Madarsas of 
Pakistan and binding on them to fall in line with mainstream of Education, to curb 
militancy and to curb the flow of foreign funds to them; has our Government 
taken any steps so far to streamline Madarsas functioning to curb I.S.I, and 
foreign funds flowing into them; 
(b) if so, the details of action taken so far; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) to (c) Madarsa is a traditional institution for religious 
education. Its regulation is primarily the concern of the State Governments. 
Relevant laws already exist to curb militancy and the law enforcing agencies keep a 
close watch on the activities of all fundamentalist organisations and institutions 
having a bearing on communal harmony and internal security and take appropriate 
action wherever necessary. 
So far as the flow of foreign funds into Madarsas is concerned, under 
the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 1976 various NGOs (including 
Madarsas) in India are permitted to recei ve foreign contribution from foreign 
sources for bona-fide activities in cultural, economic, educational, social or 
religious fields. Permission under the aforesaid Act is given only after careful 
verification of their antecedents. Funds which come through these source follow 
legal banking channels and are open to scrutiny and inspection. If any complaint 
of violation of the provisions of this Act comes to notice of the Government, 
appropriate action is taken under the law.

AFFAIRS (SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) and (b) No, Sir. However, in view of the 
low utilization of funds approved under the Non-plan Scheme for 
Modernization of State Police Forces during 2000-01 and 2001-02, the 
Deputy Prime Minister had written to all the Chief Ministers recently to

(c) "Police" is a State subject as per the Constitution of India and 
therefore it is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments to 
modernize their police forces. However, keeping in view the changing 
security and law and order scenario, particularly in the face of growing 
terrorism and organized criminal activiti es, the Ministry of Home Affairs has 
been supplementing the efforts of the State Governments in modernizing their 
police forces by way of implementing a Scheme for Modernization of State 
Police Forces since 1969-70,under which financial assistance is extended to 
State Governments for purchased weaponry, communication equipment, 
construction of police stations, outposts, police housing etc. The Scheme is 
implemeted on cost sharing basis. Central assistance is given in 50% loan and 
50% grant-in-aid. During 1969-70 to 1999-2000, a total amount of Rs. 536.74 
crore was released to various State Governments. The annual Central 
allocation was Rs. 50 crore till 1998-99 which was raised to Rs. 200 crore for 
1999-2000. The allocation was further enhanced to Rs. 1000 crore per annum 
from 2000-01 onwards from Rs. 200 crore. Accordingly Rs. 1,000 crors each 
was released to the States during 2000-01 and 2001-02 respectively. A 
statement showing the funds approved and release of Central share in 2000-
01 and 2001 -02 is given as Statement-I (See below). 
Besides the above Scheme, on account of special circumstances 
prevailing in the State of Jammu and Kashmir, the State Government is 
reimbursed amount under the Security Related Expenditure which inter-alia 
includes reimbursement for purchase of arms/ammunition, vehicles, 
security/communication equipment etc. An amount of

Increasing accident rate in metropolitan cities 
2143. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased of state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that high speed driving, unregulated traffic and 
technical flaws in the vehicles are the major causes for the increasing accident 
rate in the metropolitan cities; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether any study on roads safety aspects and nature of traffic on 
Indian roads have been conducted; and 
(d) if so, what are the recommendations of the study and what steps 
Government propose to take to implement these recommendations/ 
suggestions? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) and (b) Various reasons for road accidents are lack 
of traffic discipline on the part of drivers and road users, phenomenal 
87 

RAJYA SABHA [11 December, 2002] 
increase in the number of motor vehicles with no corresponding increase in road 
capacity, mixed traffic conditions, over-speeding, over-loading, drunken 
driving, mechanical defect in vehicles etc. However, it has been observed that 
83.5% of accidents have been caused by the fault of drivers and only 3.0% on 
account of mechanical defects in the vehicles. 
(c) and (d) Study and analysis of road accidents and implementation of 
various road safety measures is a continuous and ongoing exercise. The 
measures taken to reduce road accidents broadly are strengthening and widening 
of roads wherever necessary, improvement of road geometries, provision of 
road signages, construction of by-passes, providing training to the drivers 
particularly in the unorganized sector, publicity campaigns for awareness 
among the road users, various enforcement and regulatory measures like 
checking of overloading, checking of valid permit for driving transport 
vehicles and checking/ certifying the periodical fitness of the 
transport/commercial vehicles.

capital is very grim;

(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) Supply and distribution of 
electricity within a State is in the purview of concerned State Government/ Power 
Utility, and the instant case, it is Government of NCT Delhi/Delhi TRANSCO 
Ltd. According to Delhi TRANSCO Ltd., the power situation after 
privatization of electricity distribution in Delhi i.e. w.e.f. 1st July, 2002 is 
satisfactory by and large. During the period April-October, 2002, Delhi 
experienced an energy shortage of 1.5% and peak shortage of 2.5% as compared 
to 8.3% and 9.1% respectively in Northern Region, as a whole. 
95 

RAJYA SABHA [11 December, 2002] 
(c) and (d) In order to improve the power situation in Delhi, following steps 
are being taken by Delhi TRANSCO LtdVDelhi Generation Company/ Distribution 
Companies" : 
(i) Augumentation of transmission and distribution system at all 
voltage levels commensurate with load growth in the concerned areas. 
(ii) Action Plan for strengthening of T&D system during 10th Plan has 
already been prepared and the work is being carried out. 
(iii) Pragati Power Project is nearing completion which will provide 330 
MW power to Delhi. 
(iv) Renovation and Modernization of Indraprastha Power Plant during 
10th Plan. 
(v) Augmentation of distribution system in the critical areas under the 
'Critical areas augumentation plan'. 
(vi) Intensive maintenance including replacement Of electrical 
equipments. 
(vii) Repair, maintenance and renovation of 66/33 KV sub-stations and 
associated lines. 
In addition, the Ministry of Power in the Government of India on its part 
is taking following steps to augment availability of power and thereby mitigate 
shortage of power in the country including Delhi: 
(i) Strengthening/augmentation of sub-transmission and distribution 
network of the state system for reduction in T&D losses and 
improving quality in power supply. Project schemes aggregating Rs. 
946.46 crores have been approved under Accelerated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) for 
upgradation/augmentation of sub-transmission and distribution system 
in Delhi. 
(ii) Besides capacity addition of 225 MW in the State Sector, 
generation capacity of 7340 MW is planned during 10th Plan 
period in the Central Sector in the Northern region in which 
Delhi will also have its entitlements. 
(iii) Establishment/Strengthening of inter-regional transmission links for 
enhancement of inter-state and inter-regional transfer of 
96 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
power for optimal utilization of existing generation capacity in the 
country. Already, 220 KV Sasaram back-to-back project has been 
commissioned which has enabled flow of surplus power from 
Eastern region to Northern region of which Delhi is a constituent. 
(iv) Demand side management and Promoting energy efficiency and 
conservation measures. 
With the expected improvement in efficiency of operations due to ?bove 
steps substantial improvement in quality of power supply in Delhi is expected 
in ensuing years.

(SHRIMATIJAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) As per Central Electricity Authority 
(CEA) statistics, there are 46989 inhabited villages in Orissa (1991 census). Of

Government has released an amount of Rs. 30.00 crores to Orissa. 
  States can also access funds from Rural Electrification Corporation 
(REC), Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) and Member of 
Parliament Local Area Development Scheme (MPLADS) for the programme. 
  Rural Electrification Corporation have formulated new schemes for 
electrification of dalit bastis and hamlets at lower rate of interest.

Private companies/corporations in power distribution 
2159. SHRI DINA NATH MISHRA: Will  the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) how many State Governments have since introduced power sector reforms 
and distribution of electricity is being managed by new companies/ corporations; 
(b) how many of these new companies/corporations have started earning 
profits or have reached break-even; 
(c) the Revenue Receipts of these companies during last 12 months and 
how does these compare with the Receipts of same period in the previous 
years; and 
(d) the remedies available to the consumer for redressal of grievance related 
with deficiency in service against these private companies or corporations 
etc.? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATIJAYAWANTIMEHTA): (a) to (c) There is a general consensus 
among all States on the need for power sector reforms. In the Conference of Chief 
Ministers/Power Ministers held in March 2001. It was agreed that there is an 
urgent need to depoliticise power sector reforms and speed up their 
implementation. It was also recognized that the real challenge of reforms lies 
in distribution sector and that commercial viability has to be achieved in 
distribution through any or all of the following: 
— Creating Profit Centres with full accountability. 
— Handing over of local distribution to Panchayats/Local Bodies/ 
Franchisees/Users Associations, wherever necessary. 
— Privatisation of distribution. 
— Or any other means. 
Eight States (Orissa, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, 
Karnataka, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Delhi) have undertaken reforms 
by enacting their own Reform Laws which provide, inter-alia, for 
unbunding/corporatisation of SEBs. Distribution has been privatized in Orissa 
and Delhi. 
The reform measures including unbundling of SEBs, were undertaken by 
these States at a time when the financial health of the sector was very 
104 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
poor. The corporations/companies created as a result of reorganization of SEBs 
have shown improvements on various fronts including metering supply of 
electricity, increase in billing and collection efficiency etc. 
The distribution in Orissa was privatized in 1999 when the 
Transmission and Distribution (T&D) losses were very high, the billing and 
collection efficiency was very poor, the status of metering was not 
encouraging. Consequent on privatisation of distribution, signs of 
improvement on these and other operational levels are visible. The process of 
restructuring of electricity industry including privatisation of distribution in 
Orissa was reviewed by the State Government and it was decided that the 
upvaluation of the assets of the erstwhile State Electricity Board (SEB) may be 
kept in abeyance as it was resulting in increase in the cost of power and 
making it difficult for the sector to achieve commercial viability. 
In Delhi distribution has been privatized recently in July, 2002. Prior to 
privatisation the Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) loss levels as 
approved by the Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission (DERC) for the 3 
distribution zones taken together were at 50.7%. It is too early to assess the 
performance of these private companies in Delhi. 
(d) As per the Electricity Regulatory Commissions Act, 1998, the 
Regulatory Commissions have the mandate to inter-alia, safeguard the interest 
of the consumers. The Electricity Bill, 2001 which has been introduced in 
Lok Sabha and is presently under consideration by the Standing Committee 
on Energy makes specific provisions on consumer protection, empowering the 
Regulatory Commissions to specify performance standards of distribution 
licensees. Failure to meet the standards makes the licensees liable for payment 
of compensation to the affected person.

Problems to American Power Companies in India 
2162. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether recently during the course of interaction with an Indian 
delegation, the U.S. has voiced its co ncern over the problems being faced by 
American power companies in India in implementation of their contracts; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government in reforming and strengthening 
the distribution side of the power sector to make it financially viable? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATIJAYAWANTIMEHTA): (a) and (b) During the visit by the Minister of 
Power to the US in the first half of October, 2002, the US Assistant Secretary 
of Energy, Ms. Vicky Bailey, in her address at a symposium, stated that there 
was an erosion of confidence within the US Power Business Community about 
the Power Sector in India on account of certain contractual and payment problems 
being faced by the existing Independent Power Producers (IPPs) with US 
investments. She observed that it would be extremely difficult for American 
investors to invest in India unless structural issues in the Indian Power Sector 
were addressed. 
(c) The Ministry of Power has initiated large-scale reforms in the power 
sector. Under the reforms programme, the Ministry of Power has launched the 
Accelerated Power Development Programme (APDP) now known as the 
Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) in the year 
2000-01 as an important step towards reduction of Aggregate Technical and 
Commercial losses and restoring commercial viability of the power 
sector.Twenty-Five States have signed Memoranda of Understanding for 
undertaking reforms and restructuring in a time bound manner and linking the 
support of Government of India to achievement of predetermined milestones.To 
bring about commitment towards distribution reforms, State Electricity 
Boards/Utilities have been asked to sign a Memorandum of Agreement 
(MoA) with Ministry of Power as a pre-requisite for release of APDRP funds. 
Till now, 18 States have signed the MoA.

National Perspective Plan for R&D in Power Sector 
2163. SHRI S.M. LAL JAN BASHA: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated a National Perspective Plan for 
Research and Development in Power Sector for the next 15 years; 
(b) what are the salient features and objectives of this plan; and 
(c) whether this plan is being implemented presently? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) With a view to providing an 
impetus to R&D efforts in the Power Sector, a Standing Committee on R&D 
was set up under the Chairman, Central Electricity Authority with Director 
General, Central Power Research Institute as Member Convener. It has prepared a 
perspective research and development plan for the next 15 years in order to 
ensure optimum utilization of the research and development infrastructure by 
establishing linkage between: 
a. The basic and the applied research and development needs of 
the power sector; 
b. The national level £;)d organizational level research and 
development plans; 
to channelise the outcome of research for the benefit to the customers and the 
operational efficiency of the power sector. 
The R&D Perspective Plan identifies and prioritizes the crucial R&D needs 
required to bridge the technology gaps in various subsections of power sector 
(Generation, Transmission & Distributio n). In addition, the following policy 
issues are adui essed which are essential for formulating strategies and further 
successful implementation. 
 Need for a Nodal R&D agency to formulate strategic plans and 
partnerships. 
 Networking and Mapping the R&D resources including 
intellectual capital. 
 Strengthening the existing R&D infrastructure. 
  Nurturing the R&D human resources. 
 Funding for R&D initiatives. 
110 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
The perspective plan has identified 39 broad areas in R&D on 23 themes 
to be taken up under a short-term programme ranging from 2 to 5 years covering 
inter-alia; 
a. the measures to improve plant availability, reliability efficiency 
and safety; coal beneficiation; RLA and R&M, Green Technology 
approaches in the thermal sector; 
b. silt erosion; measures to improve plant performance renovation 
and operation and hydro-environment interface in the hydel 
sector; 
c. technologies related to solar, wind, bio-mass etc. under new 
and renewable sources of energy. 
d. grid operation and control, transmission equipment, FACTS 
advances in HVDC transmission, GIS etc. under transmission 
sector; 
e. measures to reduce T&D losses, advanced metering, 
distribution, automation, custom power devices, demand side 
management power sector reforms etc. under distribution 
sector. 
The Standing Committee on R&D has drawn an action plan for 
implementation of the Perspective Plan and is monitoring its 
operationalisation.

Corruption in Watershed Programmes 
2173. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that Watershed Programmes 
undertaken by NGOs in various parts of the country are steeped in corruption, 
in the absence of any physical audits; 
(b) if so, the facts and details thereof; 
(c) whether the grants for Watershed Programmes given by the Union 
Government to NGOs have been siphoned off; 
(d) if so, whether any physical verification of proper use of grants have 
been undertaken by Government; and 
(e) if not.the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M. K. PATIL): (a) to (e) The Ministry of 
Rural Development is administering three major Watershed Development 
Programmes, namely, the Integrated Wastelands Development Programme, Desert 
Development Programme and Drought Prone Areas Programme. Central funds 
for implementation of these Programmes by the State Governments are 
released directly to the concerned District Rural Development Agencies 
(DRDAs)/Zilla Parishads (ZPs).They, in turn, make releases to the Project 
Implementation Agencies (PIAs), which may also include NGOs among others. 
The identification and appointment of NGOs for implementation of these 
Watershed Projects is to be done by DRDAs/ ZPs. After release of the first 
instalment of Central funds along with the Sanction Order to the Watershed 
Projects, subsequent instalments are 
119 

RAJYA SABHA             [11 December, 2002] 
released only after ascertaining that the funds earlier released had been 
properly utilized for the purpose they were meant, through Utilisation 
Certificates, Audited Statement of Accounts, Project Action Plan etc. In 
addition, after a Watershed Project received 45% of the Project cost, it is 
mandatory that a Mid-Term Evaluation of the Project gets conducted by an 
independent evaluator. The next instalment to the Project is released only 
when the Evaluation Report clearly indicates satisfactory performance of the 
Project and utilization of funds as per the approved work plan. 
In the case of Watershed Projects implemented through NGOs by the 
Council of Advancement of People's Action and Rural Technology 
(CAPART), there is a system of physical audit of its programmes in the form 
of a three-tier monitoring system by independent monitors viz., pre-funding 
appraisal before sanctioning a project, mid-term evaluation during the 
implementation of the project and post evaluation after completion of the 
project. This system adopted by CAPART has prevented misuse of funds for 
the programmes.

2195. SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the reasons why the jute-bags are being reduced in use by the Central 
Government in packaging foodgrains and fertilizers; 
(b) the steps Government propose to take to give a footing to the jute 
mills in order to stand by the workers and jute growing cultivators; and 
(c) the steps Government decided to take to save the jute mills in the 
face of liberalisation of in-flow of synthetic bags and sacs from abroad?

(SHRI BASANGOUDA R. PATIL): (a) The Government issues mandatory 
packaging norms for the commodities to be packed in jute bags under the Jute 
Packaging Materials (Compulsory Use in Packing Commodities) Act, 1987 from 
time to time. Urea was exempted from the purview of the mandatory 
packaging order w.e.f. 01.09.2001 .The compulsory packaging norms for 
foodgrain has been reduced to 80% w.e.f. 12.07.2002. These orders are issued 
keeping in view the interests of jute farmers, jute industry and the end-user 
sectors.

jute mills and jute farmers, the Government is considering to launch a Jute 
Technology Mission (JTM) with the following objectives:—

cultivation;

growers to get better price for their crops; 
(iv) to increase productivity in organized jute sector, develop new 
diversified jute products and increase their market share.

the Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS). For providing incentives for 
exporters, the External Market Assistance (EMA) Scheme has been extended 
for a period of one-year w.e.f. 01.04.2002. The Duty Entitlement Pass Book

Problem of the Handloom and Powerloom Sectors in the country 
2197. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the problems being faced by handloom and powerloom sectors in the 
country; 
(b) the steps taken by Government to solve these problems; and 
(c) how the handloom and powerloom sectors workers are benefited by 
Government's policies? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OFTEXTILES (SHRI 
BASANGOUDA R. PATIL): (a) The main problems faced by the Handloom 
sector have been traditional production technique and low level of technology 
and skills, lack of modernization and Research and Development efforts, lack 
of adequate and timely supply of inputs like yarn, dyes & chemicals, non-
availability of adequate and timely credit facilities on concessional rate of 
interest. 
So far as powerloom sector is concerned, the problems being faced are 
technological obsolescence, small size of units with fragmentation, lack of 
credit availability, poor marketability, low level of skill and poor quality 
consciousness. 
(b) Looking into various problems being faced by the handloom sector, the 
Government have been implementing various schemes for the promotion and 
development of the handloom sector.The schemes include Development of 
Exportable Products and their Marketing, conducting Expos and Fairs, 
Welfare Schemes viz. Workshed-cum-Housing, Health Package, Group 
Insurance, Thrift Fund and New Insurance etc. A new Scheme, namely Deen 
Dayal Hathkargha Protsahan Yojana has also been introduced in 2000-2001 to 
cover entire gamut of activities from basic inputs and working capital to 
provisions of design, marketing, publicity etc. Apart from this, Government 
has set up National Centre for Textile Design (NCTD) to collate and disseminate 
all information related to textile weave, fabric, colour, design etc. to act as an 
electronic and regular forum to give the weavers design and marketing 
exposure. The Government has also promulgated the Handloom (Reservation of 
Articles for Production) Act, 1985 under which at present 11 categories of 
textile articles are exclusively reserved for production on handlooms. 
144 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
In order to give continued protection to the handloom weavers, the 
State Governments have been instructed to arrange distribution of hank yarn 
to handloom weavers, free of excise duty (CENVAT) through designated 
organizations which could claim reimbursement of the incidence of CENVAT 
borne by them on such yarn from the Government of India. 
The Hon'ble Prime Minister had also announced in his address to the 
nation on August 15, 2002, the facility of a one time special rebate @ 10% of 
the value of the handloom products sold, so as to enable the handloom sector 
to dispose of their stock and kick-start this employment intensive industry by 
reviving its production cycle. For this, a sum of Rs. 100 crore was 
announced.The State Governments have already been instructed to take 
advantage of this rebate and prefer their claims for reimbursement of the 
rebate amounts. The Prime Minister had also announced a scheme with an 
outlay of Rs.125 crore, for imparting training to 1 lakh weavers/artisans so as 
to enhance their skill and marketing/ managerial capabilities. Further, a 
special contributory insurance scheme for 1 Million weavers/artisans 
combining the Jan Shree Bima Yojana of the Life Insurance Corporation of 
India with Group Insurance was also announced. 
So far as powerloom sector is concerned, the Government has initiated 
a programme of modernization with induction of 50,000 shuttleless looms, 
and of 2.5 lakh semi-automatic and automatic looms in the decentralized 
powerloom sector. The TUFS has been modified so that the small-scale 
textile sector including the powerloom sector has been given an option for 
either 12% Upfront Credit Linked Capital Subsidy or the existing 5% interest 
reimbursement. 
The Government has also undertaken modernization and upgradation of 
Powerloom Service Centres (PSC), by providing upgraded equipment and 
Computer Aided Design (CAD) facility. The Government has also accepted 
the recommendations of a three-member committee of the Ministry of 
Textiles, for streamlining of management and supervision of PSCs, providing 
infrastructure and enhanced grant in aid. 
Welfare measures such as the Group Insurance Scheme and Worksheds 
have also been initiated. 
(c) As a result of the various measures taken, the handloom sector, 
which provides employment to about 124 lakh persons engaged in weaving 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [11 December, 2002] 
and other allied activities, has been able to register a ten-fold increase in 
production of fabrics from a level of 500 million sq. metres in the early 50s to 7586 
million Sq. metres in 2001-2002. This sector contributes to nearly 19% of the 
total cloth produced in the country. Exports of cotton handloom fabrics and made-
ups which were of the value of Rs.1840 crore during the year 1997-98, increased to 
Rs.2065 crore during the year 2001 -02. During the period April-July, 2002, 
exports were of Rs.851.93 crore as against Rs.667.53 crore during April-July, 
2001. 
So far as powerloom sector is concerned, it plays an important role in the 
economy of the country providing employment to about 417.9 lakh weavers. The 
number of powerlooms has grown to an estimated figure of 16.71 lakh as on 
30.08.2002. This sector contributes to about 59% of the total cloth production in 
the country.

SPECIAL MENTIONS 
Need for early completion of Teesta Irrigation-cum-Energy Project in West 
Bengal 
SHRI TARINI KANTA ROY (West Bengal): Sir, my special 
mention is on the need for an early completion of the Teesta Irrigation-cum-
Energy Project in West Bengal. 
Sir, the Teesta Irrigation-cum-Energy Project in West Bengal is one of 
the largest projects of its kind, but it remains neglected for a long period. The 
Central Government had taken up this project in early 1970s. However, right 
from the beginning, the project has witnessed unnecessary delays and it took 
more than half a decade to start the project's work in 1977. Quarter of a 
century has passed since then, but more than 65 per cent of the project 
including the left bank canal still remains untouched and the cost has 
escalated over the years. The Project began with an initial estimated cost of 
nearly Rs. 70 crores. In the subsequent years, the West Bengal Government, 
within its limited resources, spent Rs. 833 crore while the Central 
Government's contribution remains Rs. 105 crore only. According to 
estimates, Rs. 700 crore is further needed to complete the project. 
The project would provide irrigation facilities to at least nine lakh 
hectares of land in six districts of Northern part of West Bengal. It would be a 
life-line for these areas where a majority of the population belongs to 
Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes and backward communities. 
I apprehend, if this slow pace of growth continues further, the very 
objective of this Teesta Project will be defeated. 
Hence, Sir, I request the Central Government to immediately take up 
the issue on priority basis to complete the project as soon as possible. This  
would  entail  immediate  release  of  sufficient  funds  by  the  Central 
Government.

Need to Implement Second Labour Commision Report 
SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA (Uttar Pradesh): The Second Labour 
Commission in its report is believed to have recommended reduction of 
holidays, which is welcome. The productivity in Government sector is 
historically low and holidays only aggravate the situation. Compared to other 
developing countries, Government employees here enjoy a surfeit of holidays. 
The situation is out of place in a globalised environment where a nation's 
prosperity depends on the work culture of its people. The Government will do 
well to accept this recommendation. 
On many occasions holidays, which precede or follow the weekend, 
result in the stoppage of work in the Government offices for days together, 
affecting a large number of people, interacting with the Government for their 
business, travel and livelihood. A reduction in holidays will improve matters.

Its reported advice to the Centre to notify a national floor level 
minimum wage is welcome. While giving State Governments the power to fix

Request for Financial Support for Conservation of Endangered Species. 
SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhra Pradesh): Thank you, Madam. My 
Special Mention is about the need for financial support to the Laboratory for 
the Conservation of Endangered Species, set up by the Centre for Cellular and 
Molecular Biology. The Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, 
Hyderabad, has taken up an important project for setting up of a satellite 
facility for research in the area of conservation of endangered species. 
Recently, the State of Andhra Pradesh has taken the initiative in developing 
the biotechnology industry, as a basis for development, in future, in the field 
of agriculture and health. 
The CCMB, Hyderabad is one of the autonomous national research 
institutes, under the CSIR. Although primarily engaged in basic research, it 
has taken up the aforesaid nationally important project about two years back. 
This project was, up till now, supported by the Department of Biotechnology, 
and part of the fund for construction has been contributed by the Central Zoo 
Authority of India. It is now time the activities of the Laboratory for the 
Conservation of Endangered Species (LACONES) is supported on a long-
term basis, for which substantial financial inputs would be required. 
Apart from the non-recurring expenditure, the project would need a 
recurring grant for, at least, five years, to meet the cost of manpower, 
scientific equipment, consumables, services, etc. 
The Andhra Pradesh Government has allotted five acres of land, 
costing Rs.20 crores, for LACONES, for the construction facility. This would 
be a prestigious facility for the entire country and would help in developing 
technologies for improving the fertility status of wild animals, establishing

Problems of Poultry Farmers in Andhra Pradesh 
SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Thank you, 
Madam. My Special Mention is about the problems of the poultry farmers in 
Andhra Pradesh. The State of Andhra Pradesh enjoys the topmost position in 
terms of poultry production "in the country, and is currently generating 
employment to millions of people in the rural areas. Mostly, the small and 
marginal farmers in the rural areas, are dependent on the poultry sector, as 
agriculture is a seasonal activity, and is to a large extent, dependent on 
monsoon. The Government of Andhra Pradesh has recognised the poultry 
industry as one of the major engines of growth in the development of the 
State, as per the "Vision 2020" document. Presently, the poultry farmers are 
facing critical problems of high input cost and low returns for their products, 
due to a steep rise in the price of maize. The Andhra Pradesh Poultry 
Federation made a representation on the need to protect the poultry industry, 
by taking the following steps:- 
By waiving of 15 per cent customs duty on the import of maize to 
meet the growing demands of the poultry sector; and by releasing 3 
lakh tonnes of wheat from the Food Corporation of India godowns at 
export rate, that is, Rs. 4350/- per metric ton, for the poultry farmers 
in Andhra Pradesh, instead of exporting the same. 
164 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
These steps would offer much-needed relief to the poultry farmers at 
a time when there are serious drought conditions prevailing in the State of 
Andhra Pradesh. This will also result in providing employment to lakhs of 
rural people. Unemployment is an area of major concern for the State, reeling 
under drought conditions. Thank you, Madam.

SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Thank you, 
Madam, for allowing me to speak on this very complex, complicated and 
crucial Bill, which seeks to protect our nation's biological interests. There are 
three basic goals of the Convention on Biodiversity. The first one is 
conservation. The second one is sustainable use of biological diversity. And, 
the third one is, fair and equitable sharing of the benefits, arising out of the 
utilisation of genetic resources. And, under Article 6 of this Convention, we 
are required to pass this legislation, which is before the House, since we are a 
signatory to the Convention. This Bill is one of a series of Bills -- the Patents 
(Second Amendment) Bill, the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' 
Rights Bill, the Geographic Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) 
Bill, etc. -- that this august House has approved. Unless you have a proper 
linkage and synergy between the above Bills and this Bill, we can achieve 
very little through this Bill. At the same time, the provisions of this Bill 
should also be harmonised with the licensing procedures for industries using 
biological resources, such as those falling under the provisions of the Drug 
and Cosmetics Act and other related Acts. 
Madam, as the House may be aware, India has one of the richest 
biodiversity in the world. It is recorded that out of 81,000 species of fauna and 
47,000 species of flora, 15,000 species are unique to India. The Indian Sub-
Continent contains about 25,000 species of vascular plants, of which, 7,500 
are used by foreign and other traditional systems of medicine. This clearly 
shows that our Sub-Continent, particularly India, occupies a unique position 
in the world and is capable of cultivating most of the medicinal plants used in 
the modern as well as traditional systems of medicine. The medicinal 
properties of some of the Indian herbs such as turmeric, neem, etc., are most 
sought after by the multinational companies. For example, 25% of the drugs 
in the US are said to have active ingredients from Indian 
168 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
plants.   So, biodiversity is the most important, common, source on earth. But, 
now, in India, more than 1,500 species of flora and fauna are in the 
endangered category.   We have to take measures to protect them. 
While supporting the Bill, I have some reservations on some of the 
provisions of the Bill, and would like to give some suggestions for the kind 
and positive consideration of the hon. Minister, Shri T.R. Baalu, because 
unless you have a strong system, it would endanger our life-supporting 
system, the livelihood of millions of people and the very existence of 
mankind. 
Madam, I start with the Preamble of the Bill. The Preamble provides 
for conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components and 
equitable sharing of the benefits. Here, I would like to suggest the 
incorporation of the following sentence in the Preamble, namely, "And 
whereas, it is essential to ensure that no external monopoly rights are created 
on biological diversity." With its incorporation, it will be crystal clear from 
the Preamble itself that nobody would be given exclusive monopoly rights on   
biodiversity. 
Clause 2 of the Bill deals with Definitions, Madam, biological 
resources, as we know, are in the public domain. But, I am surprised to find 
that there is no definition of 'local people' or 'local community' or 'indigenous 
people.' It is, I think, because in no legislation the words 'local people' or 
'local community' or 'indigenous community' have been defined. So, you have 
also omitted that. This legislation is totally different from others because 
biological resources are directly under public domain. Therefore, we have to 
have a clear-cut definition of 'locai people' and 'local community.' If there are 
no definitions for these words in other legislations, it does not mean that there 
shbuld not be any definition here as well. So, let us make a beginning and let 
us define who are the 'local people' and which are the 'local communities.' 
Clause 6(1) deals with application for Intellectual Property Rights. It 
lays down that every person applying for any IPR has to do so with the prior 
approval of the National Biodiversity Authority. But when it comes to 
patents, the permission of the NBA needs to be obtained after the acceptance 
of the patent. Here, it appears that there is no justification for treating 
applications for patents differently from other Intellectual Property Rights. In 
my opinion, this would only leave this legislation without any teeth.   So, it 
should be made mandatory for the applicant to obtain prior 
169 

RAJYA SABHA [11 December, 2002] 
approval from the NBA before making sucn application to any patent 
authority. I also suggest that in line 36, on page 3, of the Bill, after the word 
"invention", the word "process" may be added to give more emphasis and 
appropriate meaning to the clause. 
Coming to clause 8 of the Bill, Madam, I would like to submit that 
the composition of the Board, according to the Bill, consists of Chairman, 8 
Ex-officio Members and 5 Non-official Members. Here, you are dealing with 
a legislation which is totally scientific and technical in nature and you are 
filling the Board with bureaucrats! I fail to understand the rationale behind 
this. Why does the Government want to have bureaucrats on the Board? This 
kind of an arrangement will totally defeat the purpose for which the NBA is 
constituted. This arrangement virtually gives a veto power to the bureaucrats, 
which is not proper, because they are not technical people. And, moreover, 
you have totally excluded the local communities from this provision. This is a 
clear violation of Article 8(j) of the Convention on Biological Diversity which 
places an obligation on signatories to include local and indigenous 
communities in their endeavour to protect their biodiversity. Same is the case 
with the State Biodiversity Boards under clause 22(4). Hence, the authority 
should be a high-tech body consisting of personalities familiar with 
environmental problems, biodiversity, law and other problems relating to local 
communities and indigenous people. Hence, I strongly recommend the 
inclusion of representatives from local communities. I also suggest the 
inclusion of the Director, Zoological Survey of India and the Director, 
Botanical Survey of India as Ex-officio Members on the Board. In view of 
this, I request the hon. Minister to ponder over the issue seriously and bring 
changes in the clause accordingly. 
Madam, clause 8 (3) deals with headquarters of the National 
Biodiversity Authority at Chennai. The Headquarters should be located in a 
region or a State which is rich in biodiversity and the State which is showing 
keen interest in biodiversity and other related issues. I request the hon. 
Minister to change it to a State where there are rich biological resources. 
Constitution of the Committees of the NBA is dealt with under 
clause 13 of the Bill. Under this, you have constituted only one Committee to 
deal with agro-biodiversity. I agree that many requests are going to  come 
before the NBA and the SBAs pertaining to agro-biodiversity. But, how can 
you omit other components of biodiversity, such as forest biodiversity, marine 
biodiversity, coastal biodiversity, microbial biodiversity, freshwater 
biodiversity,  aquatic biodiversity,  etc.    Hence,  I suggest the 
170 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
constitution of Committees, on the same lines prescribed under clause 13, for 
the above biodiversities to deal with the issues pertaining to them effectively 
and efficiently, and to give more teeth to this legislation. Then, the Bill 
envisages establishment of three types of funds. The first one is the National 
Biodiversity Fund, under clause 26. The second one is the State Biodiversity 
Fund, under clause 31 and the third one is the Local Biodiversity Fund, under 
clause 43. I failed to understand as to what is the need for having such a 
multiplicity of biodiversity funds at different levels. This kind of an 
arrangement will lead to utter confusion in the future. Hence, I request the 
hon. Minister to look into this point meticulously because the whole thing is 
controlled, in terms of clause 29 of the Bill, by the bureaucratic apparatus. 
Madam, these are some of the clauses on which I thought that I 
should present my views before this House, and I sincerely hope that the hon. 
Minister will reply to the queries raised by me and accept the suggestions, 
which are necessary for conservation of our biological resources, and which 
will help the local people and the local communities since biological 
resources are directly in their domain. 
With these words, I once again support the Bill and expect a positive 
reply from the hon. Minister.

Determination and Sex Pre-celection, a social action group, based in Mumbai,

Maharashtra Government to enact the first-ever law in India. The Maharashtra

legislation, based on this very Act, namely, the Pre-Natal Diagnostic 
Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act. 1994, was brought in»o 
operation from 1* January 1996. Rules have also been framed under the Act.

SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, I rise to support this Bill. We should hang our heads in shame 
that in the country of Bharat Mata, girls are killed even before their birth. 
From Vedas and other religious books, we find that women had a respectable 
213 

RAJYA SABHA [11 December, 2002] 
place in the society at that time. But now, female foeticide is increasing day 
by day. It has assumed an alarming proportion forcing the law-makers to 
discuss this problem in right earnest. Almost in every part of the country, the 
practice of female foeticide is taking place. In urban areas, female foeticide is 
done in subtle ways. In order to control this menace, we need to go deep into 
this problem. The major cause is dowry. As long as this practice is there in the 
society, this problem is not going to stop. To eradicate this social evil, we 
need to change our attitude. Law alone cannot help this. Religious leaders, 
Members of State Legislatures, social activists, and famous personalities 
should come forward to fight against this menace. In Punjab, the ratio of girls 
to boys has decreased from 882 : 1000 in 1991 to 874: 1000 in 2001. In 
Haryana also, the situation is dismal. But the silver lining in the dark clouds is 
that Akal Takht has issued a directive to the Sikh community to stop female 
foeticide. 
Another important aspect is encouragement. The Government should 
come forward and give suitable incentives to the families having girl children. 
In our State of Andhra Pradesh, the Government is already giving incentives 
to the parents having only female children. The State Government deposits 
some amount in the bank for the education of the girl child.   Besides, in 
Andhra Pradesh, women have equal property rights. 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I take this opportunity to make certain 
suggestions. The medical community needs to take this legislation seriously. It 
should necessarily target these measures in order to effectively implement this 
legislation. The present Act does not define adequately the terms, 'genetic 
counselling centres', 'gene tic clinics' and 'genetic laboratories'. Though the 
proposed amendment to the Act defines the term 'medical genetics', it does not 
define the term 'genetic science'. I also request the hon. Minister that a course 
in genetics should be made compulsory in all medical colleges and 
institutions. As far as Advisory Board is concerned, the Central Supervisory 
Board should publish half-yearly reports about its functioning, and these 
reports should be made public to ensure accountability. Similarly, the 
appropriate authorities should submit their progress reports to the Central 
Supervisory Board. These progress reports should also be made public to 
ensure greater accountability. But women who are subjected to sex 
determination tests should not be punished, because, inadvertently, in most 
cases, they are the victims. I support this Bill wholeheartedly with an appeal to 
the Government to take concrete steps for giving suitable encouragement  and 
incentives to the girl child.    The

Government should ensure that dowry prohibition laws are strictly enforced. 
Women should also have equal property rights. The sex-determination tests 
should be strictly prohibited. Wide publicity should be made through Press 
and electronic network to change the attitude of the society so that 
discriminatory practice against girls and women is abolished.   Thank you.

SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I thank you for giving 
me this opportunity to speak. 
Sir, I stand here to support the Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques 
(Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Amendment Bill, 2002. 
Sir, I would like to give certain suggestions and seek some 
clarifications. 
In the Statement of Objects and Reasons, in paragraph 3, it is 
mentioned: 
"It is, therefore, necessary to indicate and implement in 
letter and spirit a legislation to ban the pre-conception sex 
selection techniques and the misuse of pre-natal diagnostic 
techniques for sex selective abortions and to provide for the 
regulation of such abortions" 
The main aim is to avoid the technique to be used before the 
conception or pregnancy. But, in paragraph 2 of the same Statement of 
Objects and Reasons, it is mentioned: 
"The pre-natal diagnostic techniques like amniocentesis and 
sonography are useful..." 
I think after the pregnancy and maturity only these techniques are 
possible. I do not know why this has been mentioned here when it is said that 
it is to ban the pre-conception sex selection. Of course, sonography can be 
done after 28 weeks of the baby. I would also like to raise a question as to 
what is the appropriate period of pregnancy where amniocentesis is being 
done to maintain the male-female ratio. It is also mentioned in the Bill that to 
maintain the male-female ratio, we have to avoid all these diagnoses. 
Therefore, I would like to know whether this technique can be undertaken at 
the pre-conception time.   The information

put forth in the Statement of Objects and Reasons should be mentioned 
properly.   This is important in my view. 
I would also like to mention here that even nine months before the 
delivery time, when the ultrasonography is undertaken, it cannot be easily 
found that the baby is male or female. Therefore, I fail to understand why 
these two techniques have been mentioned here. I would like to mention here 
about Section 2, clause (o) found on page No.3. It says, "sex selection" 
includes any procedure, technique, test or administration or prescription or 
provision of anything for the purpose of ensuring or increasing the probability 
that an embryo will be of a particular sex;" 'Embryo' means, before 
conception, and that is why this ultrasonography is mentioned here. Section 
3B says, "No person shall sell any ultrasound machine or imaging machine...." 
I would like to suggest that the sellers must maintain a register of their sale 
{time-bell-rings) and it must be informed to the respective Government 
officials. The important point is that ultrasonography can be done for the 
reasons mentioned in the Bill. I would like to mention here, Sir, that apart 
from these reasons, there should be the actual main reason for 
ultrasonography. Sometimes, at the time of pregnancy, myoma is found in the 
uterus, which may lead to cancer. So, this reason should also be put in that 
clause.

Madam, I come to the point that the nomenclature of the Bill has 
been changed, from "Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Regulation and 
Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994" to "Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal 
Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act". The reason behind 
this change, as the hon. Member, Shri Shunmugasundaram also mentioned, is 
that the technology available in the country has forced us to change the 
nomenclature so that the general public, the para-medical and medical 
personnel, comprehend the purpose and the message of the Act from reading 
the title of the Act itself. Earlier, what was being done in the medical field -- 
as Shrimati S.G. Indira also mentioned - was, whether it was an embryo or a 
substance in the womb, we could identify whether it was a male or a female 
foetus. Now, a technology has come whereby, even without going into the 
womb or the fallopian tube or the embryo, one can ensure the conception of a 
male child. It can be done by disconnecting the 'X' and 'Y' chromosomes. 
What is done is, the *X' and Y chromosomes of a man are separated, and the 
T  c h r o m o s o m e  i s  f u s e d  w i t h  a  w oman's chromosome, to ensure the 
conception of a male child. So, because this advanced technology has come, 
the law is also required to be changed accordingly. It is with this end in view 
that the nomenclature has been changed and, also, appropriate sections have 
been incorporated in the Act. 
Then, apprehensions were expressed whether this law will also 
punish people in the case of diagnostic tests carried out for reasons other than 
female foeticide. On that, Madam, the law is very clear. So far as regulation, 
as contemplated in the Act, is concerned, we have no difficulty with regard to 
genetic and metabolic disorders; we have no difficulty in regard to 
chromosomal abnormalities or congenital malformations or sex-linked 
disorders. Certainly, the use of ultrasound machines for pre-natal diagnosis is 
a must; there is no doubt about it. But these aspects have been exempted in 
the Act itself. When discussions were held in the  Ministry, all these aspects 
were considered; there are diagnostic tests in respect of 23 contexts like 
diagnosis of intra-urine and acoptic (?) pregnancy and so on that have been 
exempted in the Act. 
Coming to medical termination of pregnancy, some Members have 
expressed doubts whether any provision is available in the PNDT Act. to deal 
with illegal and unsafe abortions. My submission is that these apprehensions 
and doubts have been addressed in the MTP Act, where penal provisions are 
available.

case of such disorders should not give an opportunity for the use of these 
machines for illegal purposes. So, the use of ultrasound machines has now

persons, one representing the police, the second person was a van driver, and 
the third person representing the public went to the spot where the caning was

the case, I would like to know whether it was correct or not that the particular 
person who represented the public, would have also informed the mob that it 
was a dead cow. I would like to know whether it was done or not. 
The hon. Minister has to go through three things. In the Statement 
the hon. Minister has said that the people in thousands armed with lathis etc., 
gathered there. Another information given is that on hearing, the police 
officers along with the force went there. The third piece of information is that 
the police decided not to open fire. The • reason attributed in this statement is

SHRI I.D. SWAMI: The State Government has also accepted the 
Report of the Commission in-toto. Not only that, even the National 
Commission on the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes made its own

of the National Commission for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes 
are almost similar, identical. Both the Inquiry Reports say that it was certainly 
not an incident of atrocities against Dalits, but, on the other hand, it was

headquarters; in each village, Dussehra festival is not celebrated, Dussehra 
mela is not held; it is held at sub-divisional or district headquarters - it so 
happened that from many villages, the people gathered there and they were 
coming back. That was the situation there. 
So far as the negligence or the connivance etc., of the police officials 
and the Executive in the State and other officers is concerned, including the 
DSP, of course, the Divisional Commissioner has also come to the same 
conclusion and the National Commission on Scheduled Castes has also 
mentioned that there was an under-estimation and they could not estimate that 
the crowd would swell so much; they had a small post, comprising of an ASI 
and 4 to 10 constables. They never expected this; but when the force came, at 
that time also, they under-estimated and that has been pointed out by both the 
reports. That is why, on the basis of the reports, all the officers are being 
chargesheeted for major penalties, not for minor penalties. Whatever other 
actions are suggested now by the hon. Members, they are for the State 
Government to consider. You will appreciate this. 
Another query which has been made is, why not an inquiry be done by 
the CBI? I am sure you will appreciate the position of law. All the hon. 
Members,  who have pointed it out, would be knowing that under the 
270 

[11 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
provisions of the law, the Central Government has no power to initiate an 
action or direct in any particular case that that should be given to the CBI. It is 
for the State Governments. If they want an inquiry in a particular case, where 
the matter, the situation, the facts are very complicated, where they feel that 
they must pass on the case for an inquiry by the CBI, then only the cases are 
sent to the CBI. Without the consent of the State Government, the Central 
Government can't transfer any case for investigation to the CBI. Of course, 
we have, luckily, in this country, not only a democratic polity but also we 
have an independent and very learned judiciary. Judicial forums are always 
available for anybody who feels aggrieved. But so far as these five families 
are concerned, I can assure you that they are satisfied. 
Of course, it was a very heinous incident, it was a very unfortunate

also there, because some of the villages surrounding that area are dominated, 
by the Jat community and other communities as well. Yes, many people are 
there from this community. 
When cases were registered against these people, when these people 
were brought, they were arrested. Then it came to light that four or five of 
them certainly belonged to the Scheduled Castes. They, are also accused in

nobody is going to tolerate it, Whatever be the area, especially in the rural 
areas. The sentiments ran.very high. That is the point. As mentioned in my
